hops.afterHeading: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope
hops.title: Why coal in sunshine still looks black
hops.text: It is natural to assume a white object always sends your eye more light than a black one. It does not. White chalk under moonlight sends less light than black coal in direct sunshine, yet chalk still looks white and coal black. Ewald Hering made this point in 1872: without constancy, chalk on a cloudy day would look like coal on a sunny day. Photoreceptors help from the start. Over a range of bright backgrounds, sensitivity falls roughly as one over the background, so they keep signaling changes relative to prevailing light. Later in the pathway, scene comparisons and cues such as surface orientation help judge surface lightness.

sources.citation: Pizlo & de Barros, Front. Comput. Neurosci. 15:681162 (2021)
McCann, Parraman & Rizzi, Front. Psychol. 5:5 (2014), quoting Hering (1872/1905)
Allred & Brainard, J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 26:949-961 (2009)

hops.afterHeading: A second question: when photoreceptors die
hops.title: Too much oxygen after the rods die?
hops.text: When photoreceptors are dying in retinitis pigmentosa, it is tempting to think the retina must be short of oxygen, and hyperbaric oxygen has in fact been used in patients. In two rat models, oxygen microelectrodes pointed the other way. As the dying photoreceptors used less oxygen, oxygen levels rose in what was left of the outer retina, while oxygen tension in the choroid, the blood supply behind the retina, stayed about the same. In transgenic pigs with retinitis pigmentosa, surviving cones show mounting oxidative damage to lipids, proteins and DNA. The authors propose that extra oxygen is what hurts them.

sources.citation: Shen et al., J. Cell. Physiol. 203:457-464 (2005)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fine glass microelectrode in a positioning stand lowered toward a small sample chamber on a lab bench beside a microscope.
image.caption: In rat models, losing rods leaves more oxygen in the outer retina; extra oxygen may harm surviving cones.

hops.afterHeading: Rescuing vision: what two gene-therapy trials can claim
hops.title: Lancelot the dog and the obstacle course
hops.text: Before any child received RPE65 gene therapy, a shaggy Briard-mix dog named Lancelot helped show it could work. RPE65 mutations in Briards cause an inherited blindness similar to one form of Leber congenital amaurosis. Lancelot was treated with an AAV vector carrying a working RPE65 gene, and the result was reported in 2001. No dog reads an eye chart, so treated dogs were tested on an obstacle course. The results were presented to the U.S. Congress. Early human trials also used a dimly lit obstacle course, and its standardized successor, a mobility test spanning 1 to 400 lux, became the main measure for FDA approval sixteen years later.

sources.citation: Acland et al., Nat. Genet. 28:92-95 (2001); Cheng & Punzo, Hum. Gene Ther. 33:865-878 (2022)
Chung et al., Clin. Exp. Ophthalmol. 46:247-259 (2018)
Cornell Chronicle, 'Gene therapy restores vision in dogs blinded by inherited disease' (April 27, 2001)
